title: The Lord stood to finish the work
word: The Lord stood to finish the work
hookLine: the Lord Himself stood to complete the saints' task, sung of the pool at Amritsar (Suhi M5, ang 783)

lines: THE LORD STOOD UP TO DO IT.
cards: Dig a hole by hand and there comes a moment. Shovel after shovel, the pile grows, and the hole seems to shrink. Then someone climbs down beside you and takes the other end.
In Raga Suhi, on Ang seven hundred eighty-three, Guru Arjan sings about a great work of digging and building: the pool at Amritsar, the work tradition says his father, Guru Ram Das, began.
And the song doesn't say, look what we built. It says something stranger. The Lord stood up to do it.

teach.b: Here's the line, paraphrased: for the task of the saints, the Lord Himself stood up; He came to have the work done.
Khaloiaa, stood up, is a picture word. Not watching from far off, not sending help: standing, the way a person gets up when the work in front of them matters.
The hymn goes on, again paraphrased: the land is beautiful, the pool is beautiful, filled with nectar water. Sikh tradition sings it of the pool at Amritsar, around which the Harmandir Sahib stands.
Now look at who gets the credit.

teach.h: REAL LABOR, AND THE HAND BENEATH IT.
teach.b: Tradition remembers builders and diggers and the sangat carrying earth: real people doing real labor. The hymn doesn't deny it. It just says whose hand was underneath theirs.
The saints had the task; the Lord stood to finish it. This path has been circling the same idea. The Bavan Akhri ended in grace.
The Mundavani laid the Name on the plate as the support of all. Here the same truth wears work clothes, dusty, with a shovel. Effort is honored, and then the one who completes it is named.
Some readers hear in this hymn permission to be finished: not because you got it all done alone, but because you weren't alone in it.

how: This hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Suhi is sung in kirtan, and some Sikhs connect it with the sarovar at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar and with seva done there.

games.q: what does “the lord stood to finish the work” mean?
o: a call to finish every task by yourself before resting
God completing the work people labor at, as at Amritsar's pool
a story of the Guru standing to lay the temple's first brick

games.q: inside the hymn: tap the pairs.

s: the hymn says the labor of the builders didn't matter
real people did real work; the hymn names whose hand was underneath theirs.
the hymn calls the pool beautiful and full of nectar water
the land is beautiful, the pool is beautiful, filled with nectar water.

games.q: the pool is finished and the sangat is gathered. you're asked to sing who did the work. what does Guru Arjan sing?
o: that the Guru built it alone.
that the Lord Himself stood up to complete the saints' task.
that the work isn't finished yet.
games.why: the saints had the task, and the Lord stood to finish it: effort honored, and the completer named.

practice: Bring to mind one task you've been carrying alone, half-dug, and sit with it a moment. Ask honestly who could take the other end of the shovel: a friend, a coworker, someone in your family.
If you pray, hold the task before Waheguru and leave it there for a breath.

wordCard.voice: The Lord stood to finish the work. For the saints' task, Guru Arjan sings, the Lord Himself stood up; sung of the pool at Amritsar. Today's word.

orig.note: stood up: the Lord rising to complete the saints' work, in Raga Suhi on Ang 783.

carryVoice: Your line: he finished it. Real labor, with another hand always beneath it. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Suhi Mahala 5, Ang 783 (santa ke karaj aap khaloiaa, har kamm karavan aaiaa; dharat suhavi taal suhava)
